finding: §2 reinstates, word for word, a precedence sentence a SHIPPED release already measured false and withdrew. §2: 'resolved through the same precedence every workflow field uses (CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in)'. spec/0.35.0.md §7 lines 569-578 says the opposite and records why: 'the precedence for workflow fields is **task override > project config > built-in**: tp exposes no CLI flag and reads no `TP_<FIELD>` environment variable for any of them, so the two upper layers named elsewhere in tp's documentation are absent here rather than merely unused' -- followed by 'An earlier draft of this section wrote the precedence as `CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in`. The audit's spec-coverage role reported, across two rounds, that the top two layers could not be verified because nothing implements them -- a claim no test can settle either way. The text now states what resolves.' Verified against the code rather than the sibling spec: engine/configresolve.go:233-269 ResolveWorkflowLayers merges exactly two layers over the built-in default (pickString([]*string{taskOverride.X, project.X}, def.X)) for every field including ReviewConvergeOn:261; and a repo-wide search for `TP_REVIEW_CONVERGE_ON|review-converge-on` returns 0 matches, so the twin this section names has neither of the two layers it claims. This is not the round-1 'no precedence is documented' finding: that one was repaired by ADDING a precedence, and the precedence added is the one v0.35.0's audit spent two rounds removing. Its cost is concrete: §5 test 1 asks for resolution 'through the full precedence chain', which is unwritable -- no fixture can exercise a CLI or env layer that no code reads -- so the release's only precedence test either asserts three layers while the spec claims five, or is abandoned.
suggestion: Replace the parenthesis with the form spec/0.35.0.md §7 shipped: 'task override > project config > built-in'. Then restate test 1 over those three layers, and add the surface sentence §7 also carries -- '`tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new field on the same terms as every existing workflow field' -- which is what v0.31.1 exists to have missed for `review_converge_on`.

finding: §1's headline measurement attributes two different corpora to one name in one sentence, and this round's rewrite introduced it: 'Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus -- 22 recorded rounds, 42 non-`PASS` rows: 3 `error`, 22 `warning`, 17 `info`.' Counted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/: v0.35.0's audit corpus is NINE rounds (audit-round-1..9.ndjson), and its non-PASS population is exactly 42 rows, 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info. The 22 is the round count of v0.35.0 AND v0.36.0 together (9 + 13), which is the same pairing §2 uses one paragraph later for the 2,913 PASS rows (1758 + 1155, verified correct). So one clause is scoped to both cycles and the next to one, under a single 'v0.35.0's own' attribution. Under the two-cycle reading the row figures are also wrong -- both cycles give 133 non-PASS rows, 18 error / 66 warning / 49 info, and 87.9% rather than 93%. It contradicts two later sections of its own file: §2.1's table row 'v0.35.0 | 9, converged' and §3's 'simulated against v0.35.0's nine rounds'. The pre-rewrite text at f9295e2 said 'Across nine recorded rounds', so this is a number the compression broke, not an inherited one.
suggestion: Write 'Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus -- nine recorded rounds, 42 non-`PASS` rows: 3 `error`, 22 `warning`, 17 `info`.' If the intent was the combined corpus, say 'across v0.35.0's nine and v0.36.0's thirteen audit rounds, 133 non-`PASS` rows: 18 `error`, 66 `warning`, 49 `info`' and re-derive the percentage, because 93% is a v0.35.0-only figure.

finding: §1 and §2.1 give opposite readings of the same measurement, and §1 never concedes the one the release actually acted on. §1: 'Two cycles in this repository and one field cycle in another project each ran long past the point where the only surviving findings were advisory' and '93% of what kept that phase open could not have blocked a release.' §2.1, on the same two repository cycles: 'v0.35.0's round 4 carries {error 1, warning 2, info 1} one round after `blocking` would have halted, and v0.36.0's rounds 7, 12 and 13 each carry `error` rows. **`blocking` would have shipped over an `error` row in 2 of 2 measured cycles.** That is decisive against it as a default.' Both are true of the corpus (verified: v0.35.0 r4 = error 1/warning 2/info 1; v0.36.0 r7 = 3 error, r12 = 2 error, r13 = 2 error) and they are true of different populations -- §1 counts ROWS over the whole phase, §2.1 counts what arrived AFTER the round `blocking` would have stopped at. The 93% therefore does not measure 'what kept that phase open': the rounds that kept v0.35.0 open past round 3 include round 4, whose error row is one of the three the 93% excludes. A reader of §1 alone concludes the loop wasted six rounds and that `blocking` is the right setting; a reader of §2.1 concludes the opposite and is the one the release followed. Nothing in §1 says the release's own measurement argues against the saving it advertises, and §1 never states the default.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §1 carrying §2.1's conclusion forward -- 'the same corpus also shows `blocking` stopping one round before an `error` row in both cycles, which is why the default stays `all` and the field is opt-in' -- and restate the 93% as what it counts: '93% of the non-`PASS` rows recorded in that phase were advisory.'

finding: §3's two paragraphs specify mutually unimplementable behaviour, and the second one has no mechanism at all. 'Mechanism' says `consecutive_clean` 'is not stored: it is derived by `engine.ConsecutiveClean` walking `AuditRounds`', and the fix is `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince`, 'which stops the walk at the first `spec_hash` boundary, and the audit path calls it.' 'Prospective only' then says 'The reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward.' A pure function walking rounds on disk cannot honour that: every round already recorded carries a `spec_hash` (verified -- all nine of v0.35.0's audit rounds carry one, seven distinct values), and the walk stops at those boundaries the first time the upgraded binary runs. Nothing in a recorded round says which binary wrote it, and §3 forbids the two ways to know: the counter is derived rather than stored, so there is no pre-upgrade value to preserve, and no new stored field is proposed. §5 test 8 -- 'rounds already on disk at upgrade keep the `consecutive_clean` they had' -- is therefore unwritable against §3's mechanism, and it contradicts test 7, which requires a hash boundary between two clean rounds to leave `converged` false on rounds a fixture just wrote. The same gap falsifies test 5: replaying v0.35.0's nine recorded rounds through 'the audit path' gives `blocking` at 8 and `all` never (simulated: the only two clean-under-`all` rounds, r8 hash 1259a4af and r9 hash 54e031e6, are separated by a boundary), not the 3 and 9 test 5 asserts. This is the successor of round 3's `mechanism-falsifies-its-own-replay`, not a repeat of it: that finding asked for the retroactive clause to be dropped, the rewrite dropped the word and did not supply anything that makes prospectivity happen.
suggestion: Prospectivity needs a discriminator or it needs dropping. Either (a) store one -- a per-round marker written from this release forward, with the walk treating an unmarked round as boundary-free, which is a stored byte §3 currently rules out and should therefore say it is taking; or (b) drop 'prospective only', accept that the reset re-reads history, and re-measure §2.1's table and test 5 under the composed rule (the numbers are 8 and never, already simulated in §3); or (c) state that test 5's replay calls the un-reset predicate directly and is a §2-only assertion, and delete any claim that it reproduces what the shipped audit path reports. In all three cases §5 needs one test that composes §2 and §3, because the composition is where the release contradicts itself.

finding: 'simulated against v0.35.0's nine rounds, which carry **eight distinct `spec_hash` values**' -- counted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json, there are SEVEN distinct values across the nine audit rounds (r1 and r2 both a46f45c6, r7 and r8 both 1259a4af; the other five rounds are distinct), giving six adjacent boundaries. The conclusion the count is offered to support is correct -- I simulated it: retroactively, `blocking` moves from round 3 to round 8 and `all` from round 9 to never -- so only the constant is wrong. It is worth reporting because of where it came from: review-r3-regression.ndjson made the same claim and then enumerated seven hashes in the same sentence, and the rewrite adopted the number without recounting. A bolded measured constant that no longer matches its own enumeration is exactly the class CLAUDE.md's 'never assert a quantifier you did not count' rule names, and this file is the release that has spent three rounds on it.
suggestion: Write 'seven distinct `spec_hash` values across nine rounds, six of them adjacent boundaries', or drop the count and keep the consequence, which is the part that carries the argument: 'no two of the rounds `all` depends on share a hash.'

finding: §4 inventories the assertions of a protected guard it deliberately reverses, and the inventory is short by one -- the one that gives the guard its power. §4: 'the guard's other assertions -- that a `wontfix` disposition does not clear an open finding, and that `--check` stays shut over a disposed finding -- are untouched'; §5 test 9: '`TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate`'s two surviving assertions still pass.' Read at internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503, the test carries THREE surviving assertion groups after the `audit_converge_on` one is reversed: the wontfix one (:485-487), the `--check` one (:489-490), and a role_streaks entry-shape block (:492-502) whose core is `assert.Len(t, e, 3, "a streak entry carries role, consecutive_clean and open only")` plus a key-presence loop. That third one is not a detail. spec/0.33.0.tasks.json records why it was written -- 'a streak-entry shape assertion that would notice a per-role threshold or a scope label arriving' -- and spec/0.34.0.tasks.json's mutation sweep records that it is the assertion that kills a mutation of this guard: 'NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate = a fourth Threshold field added to engine.RoleStreak'. Neither of the two §4 names was the killing assertion. The omission composes badly with §3, which makes the top-level `consecutive_clean` reset at a `spec_hash` boundary while saying nothing about the per-role `consecutive_clean` inside role_streaks: if the reset is to be visible per role, the closed-set assertion §4 did not count is the thing that fails, and a unit reading §4 and test 9 would meet a red gate on a guard the spec told it was untouched. The test is also on spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md:56's protected list, which §4 does not mention.
suggestion: Say three, not two, and name the third: 'the role_streaks entry-shape assertion (`Len == 3`, role/consecutive_clean/open) is untouched, so this release adds no per-role field.' Make test 9 assert three. If §3's reset is meant to reach the per-role streak, that is a change to the guard and belongs in §4 as a second deliberate reversal with its own test; if it is not, say so in §3, because two counters named `consecutive_clean` in one payload with only one of them resetting needs stating. Either way name spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md:56 as the derivation that has to move with the reversal.

finding: §2's predicate is stated over a 'surviving' set that this release explicitly declines to create, so the word means one thing in the section that defines the field and another in the Non-Goal that fences it. §2's table: '`all` | no non-`PASS` row survives'; '`blocking` | no surviving non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity'; then 'Both predicates are over non-`PASS` rows.' On the review side 'surviving' is a defined term -- engine/reviewclean.go's reviewFindingResolvedAway removes rows resolved wontfix/duplicate with evidence, and ReviewRoundClean counts only what is left -- and this section presents itself as that mechanism's twin. Non-Goal 2 says the audit side gets no such subtraction: '`--resolve` marks a row and convergence still counts it.' Verified in code: countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go) increments on `!engine.AuditRowIsPass(row)` with no disposition check anywhere. So on the audit side 'surviving' is a synonym for 'recorded', and the release's central predicate is written in a vocabulary that says otherwise three times. It is not cosmetic: §5 tests 2, 3 and 4 each say 'a round with one surviving X row', and a test author cannot tell whether the fixture's row may carry a disposition -- under the review reading a disposed `error` row makes the round clean under `blocking`, under Non-Goal 2 it does not, and the guard §4 preserves asserts the latter.
suggestion: Drop the word. Write the table as 'no non-`PASS` row is recorded' / 'no recorded non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity', add one sentence -- 'on the audit side every recorded non-`PASS` row counts; there is no surviving-set subtraction, which is Non-Goal 2' -- and restate tests 2-4 as 'a round with one recorded X row'. If the subtraction IS intended, then Non-Goal 2 is wrong and the guard §4 preserves is being reversed a second time.

finding: §3 enumerates the call sites of one function and not the other, and the unenumerated ones are the audit path's own. It says `ConsecutiveClean` 'is shared with review's `--status`, so this release **adds** `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince` ... and the audit path calls it', then enumerates only `Converged`'s reach ('`audit_record.go`, `run_status.go` and `budget.go`'). Measured across internal/ (non-test): `engine.ConsecutiveClean` has four callers -- cli/audit.go:352, cli/audit_record.go:101, cli/audit_record.go:339 and cli/review_status.go:91. Three of the four are the audit path, and each one is a printed `consecutive_clean` integer that must switch to the new function; §3 names none of them while its own rationale ('a reset that changes two printed integers while `converged` keeps the pre-reset answer is not a reset') turns on there being printed integers. The `Converged` list is right for the audit reach -- I checked budget.go:21-33, whose review branch already calls ReviewConverged and whose audit branch keeps Converged, so the split §3 proposes already exists there in the review direction -- which makes the missing half more visible, not less: the release specifies a new function for a phase-scoped predicate and leaves it to a decomposer to find the three sites that must call it, in the same release whose §1 hazard is a counter that keeps a pre-reset answer.
suggestion: Enumerate both, as §3 already does for `Converged`: '`ConsecutiveClean` is reached on the audit path by `audit.go`, `audit_record.go` (twice) and, for review, `review_status.go`; the three audit sites call `ConsecutiveCleanSince` and `review_status.go` does not.' That is also the acceptance a task can be written against, and it makes Non-Goal 4's 'review's `--status` cannot move' checkable rather than asserted. Consider instead the shape budget.go already uses -- one function with a phase parameter -- so a future audit-side predicate does not need a third twin.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught. The wrong conclusion I was about to write: '§2.2 creates an unconvergeable state -- under `blocking` the fail-closed rule makes all 67 legacy rows blocking, 51 of which (`medium` 15, `low` 36) are severities tp itself classifies as explicitly NON-blocking on the review side (engine/reviewclean.go's nonBlockingReviewSeverities), and §2.2 offers no migration, Non-Goal 2 forbids a disposition from clearing them and Non-Goal 3 forbids checking them -- so a project carrying legacy rows in its trailing rounds can set `blocking` and never converge.' It is false, and the reason is a one-line lattice check I nearly skipped: `blocking`'s clean set is a superset of `all`'s, because both predicates are over the same non-`PASS` population and `blocking` only removes rows from it. A legacy row that blocks under `blocking` already made its round unclean under today's behaviour, so the fail-closed rule can never make a round dirtier than the status quo and cannot create a dead end that did not already exist. §2.2's 'the conservative answer and needs no migration' is sound as written, and all its numbers check out against the corpus (67 out-of-enum non-`PASS` rows, high 16 / medium 15 / low 36, in exactly fifteen round files across 0.29.0, 0.30.0, 0.31.0, 0.31.2 and 0.32.0). Recording it because the shape is general and this cycle keeps meeting it: a section that repairs a false claim reads as false, and what separated the two here was checking the direction of the change rather than its magnitude.
suggestion: No spec change. §2.2 is the most defensible section in the file. If anything is added, one clause making the monotonicity explicit -- '`blocking` never counts a round dirtier than `all` does, so no setting of this field can make a previously clean round unclean' -- would retire this reading for the next reader and is a testable statement.
